A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same work, renamed from GS-Phong to MetaGS, with matching authors, method components and benchmark content. Both are readable, including v1 Appendix A and v2 Appendices A–E; their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and real-world relighting results, a qualitative OOD comparison and ablation experiments, including Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 reports original OOD, colocated, environment-map and multi-light relighting experiments, alongside ablations and in-distribution results in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 substantially revises the inner optimization: v1 separately updates Gaussian attributes with a shadow-free loss and shadow coefficients with a shadow-aware loss; v2 specifies a joint Gaussian-attribute update using Lfinal, without the separate shadow-coefficient step. The Phong/BVH backbone and three-stage framework remain. v2 also introduces an environment-map rendering procedure using sampled distant point lights.

E1.justification: Real-world coverage expands from Cup Fabric alone to seven scenes, while retaining the three synthetic scenes. v2 adds camera-light-colocated, two- and three-light, and environment-map test scenarios. OOD lighting was already illustrated in v1, but v2 evaluates it systematically across the expanded scene coverage.

E2.justification: The retained in-distribution comparison adds NRHints, WildLight and GS3 alongside the original 3DGS, Relightable 3DGS and GaussianShader baselines (v2 Table 10). OOD comparisons add WildLight and GS3 to the previously illustrated NRHints comparison, and colocated experiments introduce IRON. R3G is the retained Relightable 3DGS method under another abbreviation.

E3.justification: Reported training stages change from 10k/5k/2k to 4k/4k/5k iterations. The inner learning rate changes from 1e-8 to 0.01, and normal-prediction and flattening weights also change (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 11). New experiments introduce larger-batch controls and environment-map evaluation procedures with specially constructed baseline training data. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS remain the evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: v1's visibility-sparsity, component-smoothing and diffuse-prior ablations disappear. v2 retests the retained meta-learning and shadow-ablation questions under OOD lighting, averaging three synthetic scenes (Table 3), and adds a larger-batch control (Appendix C.2, Table 8). The qualitative decomposition comparison changes from GaussianShader versus the proposed method to full-model versus no-meta-learning results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. v2's scene averages and image error maps do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original synthetic baseline scores are retained, but the proposed method's PSNR values change from 29.51/30.04/28.73 to 30.88/32.51/31.75 (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 10). v2 adds extensive OOD, colocated, multi-light and batch-control results, while removing the original Cup Fabric in-distribution entries and several prior-specific ablation results. These are revised or newly reported outcomes, not controlled same-setting gains given the method and training changes.

T1.justification: v1's diffuse-color regularizer and analytic derivation of its per-channel scaling factor (Equations 11–12) are absent from v2, constituting a limited mathematical deletion. The standard Gaussian-splatting equations are retained in Appendix D, and the basic Phong equations remain. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: OOD generalization, already discussed in v1's preliminary findings, becomes the central problem and headline contribution in v2's title, abstract and conclusion. v2 also adds the principal claim that OLAT training generalizes to unseen environment maps, extending v1's emphasis on point-light relighting and novel-view synthesis.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the larger-batch control as evidence that meta-learning's benefit is not simply a batch-size effect. Appendix C.5 adds an explanation of NRHints' stronger in-distribution color fitting and MetaGS's advantages for irregular geometry. The conclusion adds specific limitations concerning indirect illumination, subsurface scattering and anisotropic reflectance beyond v1's generic complex-lighting and geometry caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed Blender generation settings, including camera/light sampling ranges, 512-by-512 resolution and 256 samples per pixel, plus explicit task-count and global-intensity disclosures. It omits v1's detailed regularization formulas, diffuse-prior decay schedule, baseline training budgets and dataset-license statement. The missing loss descriptions establish reduced documentation, without proving those terms were removed from the implementation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against OLAT-specific research, newly citing GS3, WildLight, RNG, OLAT Gaussians and IRON, and adding a capability-comparison table. It also adds meta-learning literature and removes several earlier references, including NeRD, Neural-PIL, NeRO and Magic123. The comparative framing increasingly distinguishes OOD generalization among OLAT methods rather than chiefly contrasting with fixed-illumination approaches.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming, the title, abstract, introduction and substantial body passages are rewritten around OOD relighting. Problem definition and preliminary findings are consolidated, standard rendering preliminaries move to Appendix D, implementation material is condensed, and related work is substantially shortened. The separate broader-impacts section is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a wider conference-style layout and extensively restructures the displays. The original OOD illustration becomes Figure 1 with GS3 added, and the model schematic is redrawn. New error-map, environment-map, multi-light and colocated figures accompany reorganized benchmark tables, expanded appendix tables and a notation table.

improvement.justification: v1's generalization claims relied mainly on comparisons with fixed-lighting-oriented Gaussian methods and a qualitative NRHints OOD example. v2 supplies systematic quantitative OOD comparisons with dedicated OLAT methods across synthetic and seven real-world scenes, substantially strengthening the central empirical argument. The batch-size control and explicit in-distribution and material limitations further improve credibility. These gains outweigh the reduced loss-function documentation and removal of several regularizer ablations, which remain material reproducibility and analysis tradeoffs.
